title: Vivekananda

cards.b:
Swami Vivekananda (1863-1902), Narendranath Datta before renunciation, was Ramakrishna Paramahamsa's disciple. He gave modern Hinduism a confident, service-centred voice and shaped the moral basis of Indian nationalism. UPSC asks about his Vedanta, nationalism, education and views on caste and religion.

His 1893 speech at the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago made him famous abroad. He founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897 to combine monastic life with relief and education.

Advaita says the one Brahman is in all. Vivekananda gave this a social turn: since God is in every person, serving the poor (daridra narayana) is worship. He criticised priests who preach renunciation while the people starve: 'I do not believe in a religion that cannot wipe the widow's tears.'

The Ramakrishna Mission (1897) was built on this: relief, schools, hospitals.

At the Parliament of the World's Religions, Chicago, 11 September 1893, he opened with 'Sisters and brothers of America' and spoke on tolerance and acceptance of all faiths, comparing religions to different rivers flowing to one sea. He rejected the claim of any one faith to be the only truth.

His book Raja Yoga (1896) and talks on Karma, Jnana and Bhakti yoga followed.

His nationalism is cultural and spiritual: India's mission is to give spiritual wisdom to the world, while learning science and organisation from the West. He urged youth: 'Arise, awake and stop not till the goal is reached' (adapted from the Katha Upanishad).

He praised physical strength: 'You will be nearer to heaven through football than through the Gita.' Aurobindo, Subhas Bose and many revolutionaries drew inspiration from him.

He attacked untouchability ('don't-touchism') and priestly privilege, and called the neglect of the masses a national sin. He believed caste as it existed was a product of history that should be dissolved by uplifting the lowly rather than pulling down the upper. He predicted the rise of the Shudras and urged women's education: 'It is impossible to think of the welfare of the world unless the condition of women is improved.'

• Dalit and anti-caste thinkers say he did not reject varna, only its abuses.
  • Neo-Hindu revivalism: used by Hindu nationalists, though he praised Islam's brotherhood.
  • Rationalists find his appeal to spirituality unscientific.
  • Supporters: a Vedantic humanist who put the poor first.

He also backed the Ramakrishna Mission's famine relief work, which shows that his service ideal was practical as well as spiritual. Critics say his Vedanta was a selective reading of the scriptures.

His definition: education is 'the manifestation of the perfection already in man'. He wanted man-making education: character, strength of mind, independent thinking, combining Western science and Vedantic spirit. The idea shaped Gandhi's basic education and National Education movements (1905).

Sister Nivedita (Margaret Noble), his Irish disciple, opened a girls' school in Calcutta in 1898 with his backing. It is a strong example of his education ideal in practice.

His birth date, 12 January, is observed as National Youth Day (since 1985). Ideas of service, volunteering and youth leadership feature in government schemes and ethics papers (GS Paper 4). The Ramakrishna Mission continues his work.

His phrase 'daridra narayana', God in the poor, is the moral base of the Mission's relief work after floods and cyclones. His call to 'arise, awake' comes from the Katha Upanishad and is often used in youth speeches.

Structure: life, Vedanta and service, universal religion, nationalism, caste and women, education, critique.

Name his lectures 'Practical Vedanta' and 'Lectures from Colombo to Almora' as sources. His death at Belur in 1902, at the age of 39, is a useful closing detail.
